claims.source: Now, when the left half of the oculomotor system is inactivated using lidocaine and muscimol injections (Aksay et al., 2007), the system can still represent right-side eye positions, but is unable to represent left-side eye positions (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data from Aksay et al., 2007 shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The oculomotor system measurements are consistent with optimal compensation and recovery boundary predictions.
claims.source: Hence, these measurements are consistent with our optimal compensation and recovery boundary predictions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claims.claim: When one neuron in the cercal system is killed, the remaining neurons do not change their firing rates.
claims.source: When one neuron in the cercal system is killed, the remaining neurons do not change their firing rates (Libersat and Mizrahi, 1996; Mizrahi and Libersat, 1997), see Figure 6F.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data from Libersat and Mizrahi, 1996 and Mizrahi and Libersat, 1997 shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The cercal system model has no redundancy.
claims.source: Indeed, our model of the cercal system has no redundancy (see Materials and methods for more details).
claims.evidence: This is explained in the Materials and methods section.

claims.claim: The cercal system exists on the 'edge' of the recovery boundary.
claims.source: The cercal system in all its simplicity is therefore a nice example of a system that exists on the 'edge' of the recovery boundary.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of redundancy and lack of compensation.

claims.claim: Orientation tuning emerges because natural images typically contain edges at many different orientations, and a sparse code captures these natural statistics.
claims.source: Orientation tuning emerges because natural images typically contain edges at many different orientations, and a sparse code captures these natural statistics (Olshausen and Field, 1996; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to sparse coding literature.

claims.claim: Polarity tuning emerges as a natural consequence of the positivity constraint.
claims.source: Polarity tuning emerges as a natural consequence of the positivity constraint, because a neuron with a positive firing rate cannot represent edges at two opposing polarities.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the positivity constraint on firing rates.

claims.claim: Without optimal compensation, the silencing of an orientation column damages image representation, especially for image components that contain edges parallel to the preferred orientations of the dead neurons.
claims.source: Without optimal compensation, (i.e., without any changes in firing rates), we find that the silencing of an orientation column damages image representation, especially for image components that contain edges parallel to the preferred orientations of the dead neurons (Figure 7B, orange arrow).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: When the population implements optimal compensation, the firing rates of many neurons change, and the image representation is recovered.
claims.source: When the population implements optimal compensation, the firing rates of many neurons change, and the image representation is recovered (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Following knockout, the preferred directions of many cells shift toward the preferred direction of the silenced cells.
claims.source: As a consequence, the preferred directions of many cells shift toward the preferred direction of the silenced cells (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The shifts in preferred direction occur in neurons throughout the population, not just in neurons with neighboring directions.
claims.source: Unlike the simple example in Figure 5G, however, these shifts occur in neurons throughout the population, and not just in neurons with neighboring directions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the high-dimensional V1 model analysis.

claims.claim: Firing rates at the anti-preferred direction also increase after knockout in the V1 model.
claims.source: As a consequence of this additional complexity, we find that firing rates at the anti-preferred direction also increase (Figure 8B,D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulations shown in Figure 8B,D.

claims.claim: Most predictions of the sparse coding model are consistent with experiments in the cat visual cortex where sites with specific orientation or direction tuning are silenced using GABA.
claims.source: Finally, although our model is simply a (positive) sparse coding model, we note that most of its predictions are consistent with experiments in the cat visual cortex, in which sites with specific orientation or direction tuning are silenced using GABA (Crook et al., 1996, 1997, 1998) (Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), while recording the firing rates of nearby neurons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model predictions to experimental data in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Neurons that escape silencing in the cat visual cortex shift their tuning curves towards the preferred directions of the silenced neurons.
claims.source: Neurons that escape silencing in the cat visual cortex also shift their tuning curves towards the preferred directions of the silenced neurons (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Neurons whose preferred direction was different to that of the silenced neurons will increase their firing rates at the knocked-out direction and broaden their tuning.
claims.source: More specifically, three types of changes were found: (1) Neurons whose preferred direction was different to that of the silenced neurons (PD>22.5∘) will increase their firing rates at the knocked-out direction and broaden their tuning (see Figure 9A, top row for an example).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Neurons whose preferred direction was opposite to the silenced neurons will increase their firing rates towards the knocked out direction.
claims.source: (2) Neurons whose preferred direction was opposite to the silenced neurons will increase their firing rates towards the knocked out direction (see Figure 9A, middle row for an example).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Neurons whose preferred direction was similar to the silenced neurons will either increase or decrease their firing to the knocked out direction.
claims.source: (3) Neurons whose preferred direction was similar to the silenced neurons (PD<22.5∘) will either increase their firing to the knocked out direction (see Figure 9A, bottom row) or decrease their firing to the knocked out direction (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations, with examples shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The V1 model finds increases in firing rates to the knocked-out directions in all three types of neurons.
claims.source: In our sparse coding model, we find increases in firing rates to the knocked-out directions in all three types of neurons (with different direction preference, opposite direction preference, or similar direction preference), see Figure 9B.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The V1 model does not observe a decrease in firing to the knocked-out directions.
claims.source: We do not observe a decrease in firing to the knocked-out directions.
claims.evidence: This is noted as a limitation of the simplified model.

claims.claim: The broad qualitative agreement between the theory and the data is quite compelling given the few assumptions that enter the model.
claims.source: Given the few assumptions that enter our model, we believe that the broad qualitative agreement between our theory and the data is quite compelling.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment by the authors of the model-data comparison.

claims.claim: Optimal compensation for neuron loss has not been proposed before.
claims.source: To our knowledge, optimal compensation for neuron loss has not been proposed before.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claims.claim: Cell loss or neuron silencing is usually assumed to be a wholly destructive action, and the immediate neural response is assumed to be pathological, rather than corrective.
claims.source: Usually, cell loss or neuron silencing is assumed to be a wholly destructive action, and the immediate neural response is assumed to be pathological, rather than corrective.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the prevailing view in the field.

claims.claim: Synaptic plasticity is typically given credit for the recovery of neural function.
claims.source: Synaptic plasticity is typically given credit for the recovery of neural function.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the prevailing view in the field.

claims.claim: Synaptic compensation has been proposed as a mechanism for memory recovery following synaptic deletion.
claims.source: For example, synaptic compensation has been proposed as a mechanism for memory recovery following synaptic deletion (Horn et al., 1996), and optimal adaptation following perturbations of sensory stimuli (Wainwright, 1999) and motor targets (Shadmehr et al., 2010; Braun et al., 2009; Kording et al., 2007) has also been observed, but on a slow time scale consistent with synaptic plasticity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Optimal adaptation following perturbations of sensory stimuli and motor targets has been observed on a slow time scale consistent with synaptic plasticity.
claims.source: For example, synaptic compensation has been proposed as a mechanism for memory recovery following synaptic deletion (Horn et al., 1996), and optimal adaptation following perturbations of sensory stimuli (Wainwright, 1999) and motor targets (Shadmehr et al., 2010; Braun et al., 2009; Kording et al., 2007) has also been observed, but on a slow time scale consistent with synaptic plasticity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The work explores the properties of an instantaneous, optimal compensation that can be implemented without synaptic plasticity on a much faster time scale through balanced network dynamics.
claims.source: In this work, we have explored the properties of an instantaneous, optimal compensation, that can be implemented without synaptic plasticity, on a much faster time scale, through balanced network dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the work.

claims.claim: The work is built upon a connection between the theory of balanced networks and the theory of efficient coding.
claims.source: Our work is built upon a connection between two separate theories: the theory of balanced networks, which is widely regarded to be the standard model of cortical dynamics (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996, 1998; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Renart et al., 2010; Denève and Machens, 2016) and the theory of efficient coding, which is arguably our most influential theory of neural computation (Barlow, 1961; Salinas, 2006; Olshausen and Field, 1996; Bell and Sejnowski, 1997; Greene et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to both theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: A tightly balanced spiking network can be derived from a quadratic loss function.
claims.source: This connection relies on the following two derivations: (1) We derive a tightly balanced spiking network from a quadratic loss function, following the recent work of (Boerlin et al., 2013; Boerlin and Denève, 2011) by focusing on the part of their networks that generate a spike-based representation of the information.
claims.evidence: This derivation is presented in the Materials and methods section, building on prior work.

claims.claim: The firing rates in spiking networks obey a quadratic loss function with a positivity constraint on the firing rate.
claims.source: (2) We show that the firing rates in these spiking networks also obey a quadratic loss function, albeit with a positivity constraint on the firing rate (Barrett et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Quadratic programming provides a novel link between spiking networks and firing rate calculations.
claims.source: This constrained minimization problem, called quadratic programming, provides a novel link between spiking networks and firing rate calculations.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical contribution of the work.

claims.claim: The work provides a single normative explanation for the polarity tuning of simple cells, tuning curves in the oculomotor system, and tuning curves in the cricket cercal system.
claims.source: In turn, we obtain a single normative explanation for the polarity tuning of simple cells (Figure 7D), tuning curves in the oculomotor system (Figure 6A,B), and tuning curves in the cricket cercal system (Figure 6E), as well as the mechanisms underlying the generation of these tuning curves, and the response of these systems to neuron loss.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the application of the theory to multiple systems.

claims.claim: Several alternative network models have been proposed that minimize similar loss functions.
claims.source: Several alternative network models have been proposed that minimize similar loss functions as in our work (Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Rozell et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2012; Charles et al., 2012; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to alternative models.

claims.claim: In alternative network models, neurons produce positive and negative firing rates or positive and negative valued spikes.
claims.source: However, in all these models, neurons produce positive and negative firing rates (Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Rozell et al., 2008; Charles et al., 2012; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012), or positive and negative valued spikes (Hu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to these alternative models.

claims.claim: The compensatory response of systems with positive and negative firing rates will be radically different from the current model.
claims.source: The compensatory response of these systems will be radically different, because oppositely tuned neurons can compensate for each other by increasing their firing rates and changing sign, which is impossible in our networks.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the differences between models.

claims.claim: Whether general spiking networks support some type of compensation will depend on the specifics of their connectivity.
claims.source: Whether general spiking networks support some type of compensation will depend on the specifics of their connectivity (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about network properties.

claims.claim: Networks designed to generate EI balance through strong recurrent dynamics will automatically restore balance when neurons are lost.
claims.source: Furthermore, networks designed to generate EI balance through strong recurrent dynamics will automatically restore balance when neurons are lost (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996, 1998; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Renart et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to balanced network theory.

claims.claim: The optimality or the speed of the compensation is likely to increase with the tightness of the balancing.
claims.source: However, the optimality or the speed of the compensation is likely to increase with the tightness of the balancing.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the network dynamics.

claims.claim: The tightness of EI balance is essentially determined by synaptic connectivity.
claims.source: In turn, the tightness of EI balance is essentially determined by synaptic connectivity, whether through experience-dependent learning of the synaptic connections (Haas et al., 2006; Vogels et al., 2011; Bourdoukan et al., 2012; Luz and Shamir, 2012), through scaling laws for random connectivities (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996, 1998; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Renart et al., 2010), or by design, via the decoding weights of linear readouts, as in our case (Boerlin et al., 2013; Barrett et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to various mechanisms for establishing connectivity.

claims.claim: The principle of optimal compensation is an idealization, and any putative compensatory mechanism of an actual neural system may be more limited.
claims.source: The principle of optimal compensation is obviously an idealization, and any putative compensatory mechanism of an actual neural system may be more limited.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the theoretical framework.

claims.claim: A series of experiments show pharmacologically induced changes in neural activities and behavior that can be explained in terms of optimal compensation.
claims.source: That said, we have catalogued a series of experiments in which pharmacologically induced changes in neural activities and in behavior can be explained in terms of optimal compensation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison to experimental data from multiple systems.

claims.claim: The advantage of the optimal compensation theory is that it provides a simple, unifying explanation for multiple experiments.
claims.source: The advantage of our optimal compensation theory is that it provides a simple, unifying explanation for all these experiments.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the theoretical contribution.

claims.claim: The theory predicts that neurons throughout the network will, on average, increase their firing rates to the signals that specifically activated the dead neurons.
claims.source: First, we can predict how tuning curves change shape to compensate for neuron loss. Specifically, neurons throughout the network will, on average, increase their firing rates to the signals that specifically activated the dead neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the theoretical framework.

claims.claim: The theory predicts that optimal compensation is extremely fast—faster than the time scale of neural spiking.
claims.source: Our second prediction is that optimal compensation is extremely fast—faster than the time scale of neural spiking.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the network dynamics.

claims.claim: This speed is possible because optimal compensation is supported by the tight balance of excitation and inhibition, which responds rapidly to neuron loss.
claims.source: This speed is possible because optimal compensation is supported by the tight balance of excitation and inhibition, which responds rapidly to neuron loss—just as balanced networks can respond rapidly to changes in inputs (Renart et al., 2010; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1998, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to balanced network theory.

claims.claim: The theory predicts that all neural systems have a cell loss recovery boundary, beyond which neural function disintegrates.
claims.source: Finally, we predict that all neural systems have a cell loss recovery boundary, beyond which neural function disintegrates.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the theoretical framework.

claims.claim: The recovery boundary coincides with a disruption in the balance of excitation and inhibition.
claims.source: We predict that this recovery boundary coincides with a disruption in the balance of excitation and inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical analysis.

claims.claim: The disruption of balance has been implicated in epilepsy and schizophrenia.
claims.source: This has not been explored experimentally, although the disruption of balance has recently been implicated in a range of neural disorders such as epilepsy (Bromfield, 2006) and schizophrenia (Yizhar et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claims.claim: The properties of a recovery boundary may shed light on the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.
claims.source: Indeed, the properties of a recovery boundary may also shed light on the progression of neurodegenerative diseases—especially those that are characterized by a period of asymptomatic cell loss, followed by a transition to a disabled symptomatic state, as in Alzheimer's disease and stroke (Leary and Saver, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative application of the theory to disease progression.

claims.claim: The transitions from asymptomatic to symptomatic states may occur at the recovery boundary of the diseased system.
claims.source: We speculate that these transitions occur at the recovery boundary of the diseased system.
claims.evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claims.claim: An accumulation of asymptomatic damage will increase the susceptibility of the brain to symptomatic damage by moving it closer to the recovery boundary.
claims.source: If this were the case, then an accumulation of asymptomatic damage, through aging for example, or through acute conditions such as silent stroke, will increase the susceptibility of the brain to symptomatic damage, by moving it closer to the recovery boundary.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the recovery boundary concept.

results.result: The manuscript presents background claims about neural resilience to damage, including that neurodegenerative diseases can remain asymptomatic for years, most strokes are silent, and partial lesions often fail to produce behavioral effects.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C7-C10) are well-supported by citations to prior literature (Morrison and Hof 1997; Leary and Saver 2003; Li et al. 2016) and represent established knowledge in the field. The claims provide appropriate context for the study's motivation.

results.result: The authors propose the principle of optimal compensation, defined as the change in firing rates necessary to remain at the minimum of a loss function after neuron loss, which relies on redundancy in neural representations.
results.evaluation: The theoretical framework (C3, C20-C22) is clearly defined and logically consistent. The definition of optimal compensation is mathematically precise, and the requirement for redundancy follows logically from the constraint that multiple firing rate combinations must represent the same signal.

results.result: Optimal compensation can be implemented through balanced network dynamics without synaptic plasticity, where networks are wired such that firing rates evolve to minimize a loss function through spike-by-spike balance of excitation and inhibition.
results.evaluation: The mathematical derivations (C84-C86) connecting spiking networks to loss function minimization are presented in detail in Materials and Methods. The claims are supported by prior theoretical work (Boerlin et al. 2013) and extended through quadratic programming with positivity constraints, providing a novel contribution.

results.result: In simulated spiking networks, when neurons are lost, the remaining neurons automatically increase their firing rates to restore excitatory-inhibitory balance, which guarantees continued accurate signal representation.
results.evaluation: The simulation results (C30-C37) are demonstrated in Figures 1-2 with clear evidence of firing rate increases and balance restoration. The mathematical relationship between E/I balance and signal accuracy is proven in Materials and Methods, providing strong support for these claims.

results.result: Neural systems have a recovery boundary beyond which compensation fails, characterized by disruption of excitatory-inhibitory balance and inability to correct representation errors, occurring when neuron voltages run out of bounds.
results.evaluation: The recovery boundary concept (C6, C16, C39, C41-C43) is demonstrated through simulations in Figure 3 showing voltage aberrations and E/I ratio disruption. The theoretical characterization is consistent with the network dynamics, though experimental validation of the predictions (C101-C102) is limited.

results.result: Networks can withstand loss of many more neurons when knockout is random rather than systematic.
results.evaluation: This claim is clearly demonstrated in Figure 3J showing that random knockout allows the network to maintain function until only a few neurons remain, compared to earlier failure with systematic knockout. The result is logical given that random knockout preserves representational diversity.

results.result: The positivity constraint on firing rates (neurons can only have positive firing rates) fundamentally alters compensation mechanisms and produces piecewise linear tuning curves with non-linearities, including polarity tuning in visual neurons.
results.evaluation: The claims (C26-C27, C47-C50, C62) are well-supported through quadratic programming analysis shown in Figure 4 and mathematical derivations. The emergence of piecewise linear tuning curves and polarity tuning as consequences of positivity constraints is a novel theoretical insight with clear mathematical justification.

results.result: Following neuron knockout, similarly-tuned neurons increase firing rates while dissimilarly-tuned neurons decrease firing rates, with neurons shifting tuning curves toward preferred directions of missing neurons, resulting in substantially better representation than without compensation.
results.evaluation: These predictions (C51-C53) are clearly demonstrated in Figure 5 simulations, showing both the direction of firing rate changes and the improvement in representation error. The results are consistent with the optimal compensation principle and provide testable predictions.

results.result: The model predictions for the oculomotor system match experimental observations, including recruitment order of neurons and the ability to represent ipsilateral but not contralateral eye positions after unilateral inactivation.
results.evaluation: The comparison to oculomotor data (C54-C57) from Aksay et al. (2000, 2007) shows good qualitative agreement between model predictions (Figure 6B) and experimental measurements (Figure 6A,C). The consistency supports the optimal compensation framework, though this is post-hoc model fitting rather than a priori prediction.

results.result: The cricket cercal system shows no compensation after single neuron loss because the model has no redundancy, representing a system at the edge of the recovery boundary.
results.evaluation: The cercal system analysis (C58-C60) is supported by experimental data (Libersat and Mizrahi 1996; Mizrahi and Libersat 1997) showing no firing rate changes after neuron loss. The interpretation that this reflects lack of redundancy (N=4, M=2) is consistent with the theoretical framework.

results.result: In a high-dimensional V1 sparse coding model, optimal compensation after orientation column silencing recovers image representation through widespread changes in firing rates and shifts in preferred directions throughout the population, including increases at anti-preferred directions.
results.evaluation: The V1 model results (C61, C63-C67) are demonstrated in Figures 7-8 with clear evidence of representation recovery and tuning curve shifts. The complexity of high-dimensional compensation is well-characterized, though the model is simplified (positive sparse coding without some biological constraints).

results.result: The V1 model predictions are largely consistent with cat visual cortex experiments showing tuning curve shifts toward silenced directions, though the model does not capture all experimental observations (e.g., decreases in firing for some similarly-tuned neurons).
results.evaluation: The comparison to cat V1 data (C69-C76) from Crook et al. (1996-1998) shows broad qualitative agreement for three types of neurons, but the model fails to reproduce firing rate decreases observed experimentally (C75). The authors acknowledge this limitation and attribute it to model simplification. The agreement is compelling given few free parameters, but the mismatch indicates incomplete understanding.

results.result: The theory predicts that compensation occurs through increased firing rates to signals that activated dead neurons, happens extremely fast (faster than spiking timescale) due to tight E/I balance, and can be tested experimentally.
results.evaluation: These predictions (C98-C100) follow logically from the theoretical framework and network dynamics. The speed prediction is supported by balanced network theory (citations provided). However, these remain untested predictions requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: Optimal compensation for neuron loss is a novel theoretical framework that differs from prevailing views emphasizing synaptic plasticity, providing a unifying explanation for multiple experimental observations.
results.evaluation: The novelty claims (C77-C79, C82, C97) are supported by the lack of prior work on instantaneous optimal compensation. The framework does provide a parsimonious explanation for diverse phenomena, though the claim of complete novelty should be tempered by related work on balanced networks and efficient coding.

results.result: The work builds on efficient coding theory, which has successfully explained observations in vertebrate and invertebrate sensory systems, by connecting it to balanced network theory.
results.evaluation: These background claims (C12-C14, C83) are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The connection between efficient coding and balanced networks is a genuine theoretical contribution, though both frameworks existed independently before this work.

results.result: Alternative network models that allow negative firing rates will show radically different compensation, and general balanced networks may compensate depending on connectivity, with tightness of balance determining compensation quality.
results.evaluation: The discussion of alternative models (C88-C94) is well-reasoned and supported by citations. The logical argument that oppositely-tuned neurons with negative firing rates would compensate differently is sound. The connection to balanced network theory is appropriate, though the claim about optimality increasing with balance tightness (C93) is speculative.

results.result: The recovery boundary concept may explain disease progression in neurodegenerative conditions, where asymptomatic cell loss transitions to symptomatic states, and accumulated damage increases susceptibility by moving systems closer to the boundary.
results.evaluation: These speculative claims (C103-C106) about disease implications are explicitly labeled as speculation by the authors. While the recovery boundary concept is theoretically sound, its application to Alzheimer's disease and stroke progression lacks direct experimental support. The citations (C103) to E/I imbalance in epilepsy and schizophrenia provide only indirect support.

results.result: While optimal compensation is an idealization, the framework explains pharmacologically-induced changes across multiple experimental systems.
results.evaluation: The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C95) while demonstrating broad applicability (C96) through comparisons to oculomotor, cercal, and V1 systems. This balanced assessment strengthens rather than weakens the work's credibility.
